extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and people interested in document forensics or the 2004 political controversy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and indicators used to assess whether historical memos are authentic or forgeries, with emphasis on typographic, formatting, content, and forensic-expert comparisons. Focused on the Killian memos but applicable to forensic examination of purportedly historical documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for original documents for professional authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of authenticity is not possible without original documents; CBS used only faxed and photocopied duplicates, so authentication to professional standards would be impossible regardless of provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because only photocopies/faxed duplicates were available, professional authentication (positive verification) cannot be performed; however, proving documents inauthentic does not depend on availability of originals — copies can show anachronisms or features inconsistent with the alleged era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typography (general) — typewritten appearance vs word-processed
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial doubts centered on the fact that the memos did not look like typical typewritten documents and appeared very similar to documents produced with modern word-processing software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare visual characteristics of the questioned documents to known exemplars from the era; consult multiple typographic and forensic experts. Note that bloggers first raised these issues and mainstream press sought multiple expert opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of proportional fonts (as opposed to a monospaced typeface) — most typewriters in 1972 used fixed-width fonts; authenticated TexANG documents were typed using fixed-width fonts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of proportional spacing techniques characteristic of modern word processors is suspicious. Some experts gave counterclaims that certain IBM machines could produce similar spacing, but detailed comparison of letter widths and spacing can distinguish mechanical typewriter outputs from modern fonts. The Washington Post noted none of >100 records from the 147th Group used proportional spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-character spacing / kerning
rubrics_metrics.description: The memos display kerning/character-spacing behavior characteristic of TrueType fonts (e.g., 'fr' pair behavior) not available on office equipment in 1972.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for kerning adjustments (characters moved closer, tucked under others) that are typical of digital fonts. Experts like Joseph Newcomer argued these features make the documents 'necessarily forgeries.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Letterspacing and character-width systems (technical measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Times New Roman in modern Word employs an 18-unit system relative to em; early 1970s proportional typewriters used a narrower system (e.g., IBM Selectric Composer used 9 units). Differences in character widths accumulate over line length, producing detectable mismatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure relative character widths and accumulated line endings; if letterspacing matches modern 18-unit patterns rather than mechanical 9-unit (or fewer) patterns, the document likely could not have been produced by early-1970s mechanical typewriters and is likely a modern creation (phototypeset or hot-metal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Centered headers alignment consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Centered headers produced on a typewriter (by counting and adding spaces) can vary between occasions depending on paper insertion, while word processors center based on a fixed central reference, producing identical centering across pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlaying the memos with word-processor-produced blocks: exact matches of centered lines across documents produced months apart suggest word-processing production rather than manual centering on a typewriter. However, manual methods (and some typewriters with kerning keys) can produce consistent centering if the same procedure is strictly repeated; evaluate probability and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curved apostrophes and smart quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents use apostrophes curved to the left and curved/angled quotation marks (smart quotes) rather than the vertical straight apostrophes and straight quotes typical of typewriters of the era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check glyph shapes: angled/curved single and double quotation marks (and distinct opening/closing quote glyphs) are indicative of modern word-processing typography; typewriters generally used straight vertical apostrophes/quotes. Presence of smart quotes in copies is suspicious for pre-1980s typewritten memos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity to contemporary documents from the same source
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison with over 100 records made available by the 147th Group showed none using the proportional spacing techniques seen in the CBS documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate questioned documents against a corpus of contemporaneous, authenticated documents from the same office/unit to determine whether formatting/typographic features are consistent with the office's normal practice and available equipment. Lack of similarity raises likelihood of forgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and formatting consistency with office practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspects such as content phrasing, terminology (e.g., Army vs Air Guard terms), formatting choices, and presence/absence of signatures were scrutinized; Killian's family and others disputed that he would use typewriting equipment or keep such memos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze internal content for terminology consistent with the issuing office, examine habitual practices (handwritten vs typed memos), and cross-check claims from family, former secretaries, and colleagues about the subject's habits. Discrepancies in expected practice and actual document features are indicators of potential inauthenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature authenticity and limitations due to copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one memo bore a full signature; CBS said a document examiner determined the signature was authentic, but the examiner later said he could not authenticate copies far removed from originals. Other examiners gave 'limited opinions' that Killian did not sign or initial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when authenticating signatures from photocopies or faxes; experts may refuse to authenticate distant copies. Seek original signatures/exemplars where possible; if originals unavailable, understand that signature opinions are limited and uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content anachronisms and factual inconsistencies (personnel, dates, events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific content issues: memos cite pressure by Walter Staudt though he retired before the cited action; flight-inquiry references lack supporting records though regulations required such reviews; a May 4, 1972 order required a report date that fell on a weekend/Mother's Day when the base was closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check factual claims and referenced events/dates against independent official records, personnel service records, and institutional calendars. Anachronistic references, impossible timelines, or references to individuals not in the stated role at the time are strong indicators of inauthenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forensic expert device comparison (Peter Tytell analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peter Tytell's analysis (for the CBS review panel) concluded: (i) a relevant exemplar was produced on an Olympia manual typewriter, (ii) the Killian documents were not produced on an Olympia manual typewriter, and (iii) the Killian documents were produced on a computer in Times New Roman typestyle — therefore not produced on a typewriter in the early 1970s and not authentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform device-level comparisons between questioned documents and exemplars produced on candidate machines/software. Experts should test whether the questioned documents' typographic and spacing characteristics can be replicated by the alleged production technologies. A conclusion that the documents match modern computer fonts (e.g., Times New Roman) and cannot be reproduced by contemporaneous devices supports a finding of forgery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability judgment supported by lack of plausible contemporaneous production method
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts concluded that the matching letterspacing of the Killian documents could only have been produced using phototypesetting or hot-metal printing at the time they were purportedly created; since it is unrealistic that Killian would have had documents printed that way, the memos are almost certainly modern forgeries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider not only technical matches but also plausibility: whether the purported author/office would have had access to the specialized production methods implied by the document's features. If a technical production method is inconsistent with plausible access, that strengthens an inference of forgery.
